Lessons.Title: Rewriting Quadratic Expressions in Factored Form (Part 3)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: recognize quadratic expressions without a linear term as differences of squares, justify the factorization a²−b²=(a−b)(a+b), and distinguish real factorability from sum-of-squares forms. Original Edulytiks adaptation aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 8 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/8/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/8/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source's number-pattern warm-up uses products of numbers equally spaced around a center.

Original algebraic examples x²−49=(x−7)(x+7) and 4x²−25=(2x−5)(2x+5). When expanded, cross terms cancel: x²+7x−7x−49=x²−49. This explains the missing linear term rather than treating it as a coincidence.

Number identity examples 9×11=(10−1)(10+1)=100−1=99 and 19×21=(20−1)(20+1)=400−1=399 show the same structure. By contrast x²+49 cannot be written as (x−7)(x+7) over reals, because that product gives x²−49.

Student task: find the center of several near-square products, expand both signed binomials in an area/equation representation, factor two difference-of-squares polynomials and critique a proposed factorization of a sum of squares. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for structural recognition, exact algebra, mental computation and counterexample reasoning.

SummaryPoints: Difference of squares is a special no-linear-term factor pattern.
Cross terms disappear because of opposite signs.
The identity also accelerates near-square arithmetic.
Teacher reviews proof and contrasting sum-of-squares case.
